*We dedicate this book to all the community and professional organizations that  serve the Latino community. It is through the tireless efforts and sacrifices of  the individuals that work in these organizations that many Latinos are able to  attain the skills that lead to innovation success.*  
**Abstract** 

This book is a study on how Latino culture in the United States views,  defines, and can help lead innovation. Achieving sustainable innovation  success is a concept many corporations struggle to attain. The authors  have found through their research that very often it is a result of too much  effort being directed at processes rather than focusing on the source of  innovation—its human capital. Realizing that innovation emanates from  human beings and people view innovation differently based on their cul tural upbringing, the authors present their findings and recommenda 

tions in a practical manner on the fastest growing demographic in the  United States.  

Since the 1980s the United States Latino population has been on a  steady growth path that has established this group as the largest “minority”  in the country. Growth projections show no slow down and the group  will make up a significant portion of the U.S. workforce for decades to  come. Consequently, Latinos are positioned to assume roles of greater  responsibility in corporate America. Thus, it is important to understand  how to prepare, recruit, and position knowledge workers with this cul tural background to contribute innovation successes to their firms. 

The material is written to reach a wide audience. Thus, it presents  macro data for those unfamiliar with this demographic, while also provid ing original research on attitudes, opinions, and disposition of Latinos to  innovation from the Project Impact study.  

**Keywords** 

innovation management, Latinos, Hispanic professionals, workforce  development, human capital, multicultural marketing, diversity

**Preface** 

This is a book about how Latinos view and define innovation. As innova tion has become an essential part of global competitive strategy, it has also  become a concept that can be confusing because of its many meanings  and interpretations. Using the research and work of our Project Impact  study, we have been able to uncover patterns in how different cultures  define innovation. Here we are focusing our efforts on Latinos, a group  that plays a significant role in how the United States will be positioned to  compete with other nations for decades to come. 

The impact that Latinos are having on the U.S. society, in particular,  is significant. What began as, and still is, a movement of immigrants com ing to the United States and chasing the “American Dream” is quickly  turning into the story of a group of people who will emerge as a lead ing force in American competitiveness in the 21st century. The Latino  story can be seen in a range of books that chronicle the “Chicano” story,  while also telling us about the struggles of Cuban refugees who left their  families on the island, but created viable and sustainable businesses in  the United States. We have also seen the literature transition from stories  of individuals conquering obstacles in their daily lives to books on how  to sell to the Latino market or how to hire Latino talent. The Latino  story also continues to grow and mature as we begin to see professional  development and networking organizations such as the Hispanic Alliance  for Career Enhancement (HACE) and the National Society of Hispanic  MBAs (NSHMBA) go beyond early education and form professional net 

works for career development. 

This brings us to this book, and an unlikely trio of authors who are  combining their knowledge and experience to deliver the next genera tion of management literature to lead a multicultural workforce. The trio  is unlikely in that almost all books that are written about Latinos are  by Latinos. This is certainly understandable, but it brings an exclusively  Latino perspective. Our society is blending, and eventually those who are  currently considered minorities will become the majority, and Latinos   
xiv Preface 

are interacting, leading, and working with people of all backgrounds.  So, why not share the experiences of others in understanding innovation  from a cultural perspective? 

This book could certainly have been written exclusively from a Latino  (Vinny’s) perspective. But that approach would have ignored the reality  that successful businesses do not operate in silos, even more so in regard  to leveraging the innovative capabilities of a multicultural workforce.  Thus, it led to the writing of this management-themed book addressing  the need for corporations to understand that culture does impact innova 

tion efforts. Consequently, innovation must be approached with a scien tific perspective that also integrates practical application. We share our research from our Project Impact study as well as our  practice-based ENOVALE™ framework. This work narrows down to  defining innovation as how it is perceived (understood) by the individual.  From this, our research identified three ways innovation is encountered  (experienced): 

• A new product, technology, or service 

• An improved product, technology, or service 

• A product, technology, or service changed for the positive 

Using this as a foundation, organizations can build their programs by  aligning their teams for innovation success. We will show the results  of our research in regard to Latinos throughout North America and  South America in this book and how these groups integrate to form a  cohesive unit. 

We have taken a strategic approach in developing this work, because it  is important in building a national innovation infrastructure. The Latino  demographic is most associated with growth, popular culture influences,  and a strong potential market segment. It is rarely associated with inno 

vation. Thus, we provide a background of how this demographic has  emerged, we share our original research, illustrate with examples, and pro vide recommendations on how to leverage the capabilities of this group  for innovation. It is our intent to provide you a foundation for identify ing, defining, aligning, and embedding innovation culture throughout  your organization. In this book (our third book), we are bringing you our   
Preface xv 

insight into the development of the Latino workforce to leverage innova tion. Latinos are the single greatest ethnic group to acculturate into the  United States. Their contribution to the growth of the U.S. economy  and to American competiveness will require Latinos to assume positions  of greater responsibility with more emphasis on developing innovative  capabilities.   
**CHAPTER 1** 

**Latinos Emerge** 

To understand how culture impacts innovation, it is important to have  a fundamental understanding of the culture with which one is working.  This chapter serves to inform you about the history, size, and makeup  of Latinos within the United States. The intent is to provide you with a  descriptive overview of this dynamic demographic segment. 

**Latinos in the United States** 

The impressive growth in the U.S. Latino population during the last two  decades has impacted U.S. culture, politics, business, and American com petitiveness. This group’s cultural influence can be seen in music, food,  and even the language. One way or another, this group has created busi nesses and jobs and has established a consumer buying power estimated  at over a trillion and a half dollars as of this writing. This figure is larger  than the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) of most Latin American econo mies. Influence on corporate America is also growing, with more Latinos  occupying senior management and board positions. Combined, all these  elements indicate that Latinos are in a position to become the face of  

American competitiveness and innovation in the 21st century. As of this writing, the U.S. Census Bureau of 2010 estimates the His panic population to be over 52 million strong or 16.7% of the total popu lation. Between 2008 and 2009, the population grew by 1.4 million, and  a year later it increased by another 2.5%. Impressive numbers indeed, and  when we look at the total Latino population estimate of 132.8 million by  2050 from a starting point of 22.5 million in 1990, we can get a sense of  the importance of this demographic for U.S. competitiveness. Using this  for context, we can frame our discussion to build an infrastructure that  will help this next generation of knowledge workers maximize its innova tive capabilities.  
2 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

This demographic is currently young and characterized by a propen sity to have large families. In 2010 there were an estimated 10.7 million  Hispanic households in the United States and 61.1% of them had chil dren under the age of 18\. Hispanic children under the age of 5 made up  26% of all children of that age. Consequently, these societal influences will  continue, because demographic projections show that more than one in  every four Americans (30%) will be of Hispanic descent by 2050\.1 By that  year, projections show the total Latino population to be around 132 mil lion and this group will comprise over a third of the U.S. workforce. This  large demographic has the potential to be the largest organic provider of  American knowledge workers and the source of future American competi tiveness; thus, it is a vital part of sustained American prosperity. Therefore,  this book is written to provide insight into the factors that impact the  Accelerators and Barriers to the innovative capabilities of this group. 

The changes that the United States is undergoing in its demographic  makeup will continue to have an impact on culture in society and in  the labor force. This shift in the U.S. workforce brings new generational  and ethnic influences and introduces new approaches to processes in the  workplace. Couple this with a business environment that is more glob 

ally interconnected and culturally diverse, and you find an environment  that requires business and government to look at their policies differently,  and to adopt new processes and methodologies as well. In the United  States, the reaction to these changing dynamics has been addressed mostly  through Diversity and Inclusion (D\&I) efforts, and multicultural segmen 

tation in marketing. D\&I efforts of bringing in diverse representation and  establishing an inclusive environment are no longer sufficient. It is actu ally expected, and after years of making efforts to create a more inclu sive and diverse environment, many companies are asking “now what?”  They believe they have made the workforce more diverse but how do  they improve business results? That is, how do they achieve a competitive  advantage? Many approaches are being pursued, but the key to successfully  

competing on a global scale is by unlocking innovation in organizations. In our research through Project Impact, a global study on how cul ture impacts innovation, we have found that all innovation begins and  ends with the individual. Innovation emanates from human beings.  Understanding, capturing, and harnessing the power of how people   
Latinos Emerge 3 

think, react, and create is critical to all innovation development. People  are different in the way they think by the nature of their upbringing and  surroundings. Circumstances will dictate how they react to their environ ment. Attitudes, opinions, and disposition toward innovation are unique  attributes that will differentiate people. Thus, the circumstances by which  Latinos have come to the United States, and the environment they have  experienced have shaped thinking and innovative capabilities. It is this  new look of the American workforce that will compete with the rest of the  world, and it is important to understand what makes this group unique. 

One important consideration in understanding Latinos is that this  demographic is also changing. It is not as easy to identify this demographic  based on the country of origin, as was the case in the 20th century. The  newer generation of Latinos has in many cases lost any ties to their home  country and has been fully acculturated. They have also mixed with other  Americans, resulting in the creation of a culture that is now uniquely  American. Compounding this situation further is a workforce that is more  multigenerational than ever before. The Baby Boomer generation (individ uals born between 1946 and 1964\) is staying on longer and fulfilling other  roles while Generation Xers (individuals born between 1965 and 1979\)  begin to replace them in leadership positions, and Millennials (individuals  born between 1980 and 1999\) begin to establish themselves by building  upon an established foundation or recreating the business environment. 

In our first two books, we provided a framework for unlocking inno vation success in any organization using the ENOVALE™ methodology.2 This methodology is one that is based on the premise that all innovation  emanates from human beings. Consequently, by identifying how dif ferent people define innovation, an organization can establish a path to  achieving a sustainable competitive advantage. In this book, we are going  back to our roots to explore culture as an essential element impacting  innovation, by addressing U.S.-based Latinos. We will study the impact  this group has in the United States from three perspectives: 

• First, through a marketing lens 

• Second, from an elections and policy development view • Third, from how it is shaping the U.S. workforce and global  competitiveness perspective  
4 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

The third point will receive the most attention and serves as the focus of  this book, but the other factors provide the contextual background to  show how this demographic has emerged into prominence. 

In recent years, there has been an increase in Latino or Hispanic themed  books3 and articles. The majority of these efforts are focused on historical  events that have led to the establishment of the Latino community in the  United States. Others have taken a narrative approach to highlight the rich  cultural heritage and contributions that Latinos have made to the United  States. There are a plethora of inspirational studies that show how Latinos have  overcome great adversity to achieve the “American Dream,” and how they have  influenced or permeated American society. But there are also many examples  of the struggles Latinos still face. This provides us with an understanding of  the makeup of Latinos in the United States. From a marketing perspective, sig nificant literature can be found that is directed to reaching and understanding  the Latino market with the intent of growing certain consumer brands. There  is also a significant amount of work that has come from the D\&I community  that looks at attracting and developing Latino talent. None of these efforts ade quately address how to unlock the innovative capability of this demographic. 

Innovation is currently the most sought out strategic platform for  organizations, in the developed world and emerging markets, to differen tiate themselves and achieve global competitive advantage. Consequently,  we are seeing numerous countries investing in their innovation ecosys tems to compete against each other to attract the world’s global enter prises. Take Colombia and its investment in Science, Technology, and  Innovation (CTI in Spanish) investments such as “Ruta N” in Medellin,  or Innovation Academies in China. Many of these countries have a mostly  homogenous culture that makes directing innovation initiatives less com plex. This is not the case in the United States. We are multicultural and  multigenerational, and there are many factors that influence the develop ment of our innovation ecosystem. We will address these points in this  book with a focus on the fastest growing demographic—Latinos. 

**Who Is a Latino?** 

Latinos or, the less frequently used term, Hispanics are U.S.-based indi viduals who come from Spanish speaking countries in Central and South   
Latinos Emerge 5 

America, and the Caribbean. This region is often referred to as Latin  America (LatAm). Although those from Spain and Brazilians are some times placed into this group, it is not an exact fit, because the cultural  background for immigrants from these countries is European for Span iards; and the Brazilian population draws its heritage from a Portuguese  perspective. However, Brazil has uniquely its own culture that does not  exactly fit into any category other than Brazil. Consequently, Hispanics  may be a more precise definition, but we will mostly use the more popular  Latino term throughout the book for simplicity. Consequently, we use  both terms interchangeably. However, Brazilians do make up a part of the  Latino culture, yet are considered different due to language and cultural  ties to Portugal. 

Brazilians are the group of Latinos who in the United States are nor mally not included in the mainstream of Latino conversations. But as the  general population is becoming more familiar with Latinos of Spanish  speaking descent, they are less informed on Brazilians. So we thought  we’d spend a little time with this important demographic. 

Brazilians draw their heritage from the Portuguese. This is unique in  that it is the only Portuguese speaking country in South America. The  country has nearly 200 million residents and geographically the size of the  United States. Blessed with many natural resources, the country is now  beginning to emerge as a global economic power, ranking as the world’s  fifth largest economy. Nevertheless, they do have a significant presence in  the United States. 

Brazilians in the United States are primarily concentrated in Miami  and the Northeast. An estimated population of 300,000, they still par ticipate in many events oriented toward Latinos, but also can be very  helpful in understanding the bigger consumer market that is Brazil. They  can be viewed in three categories, according to Ana Dutra, Executive Vice  President at an executive search firm Korn Ferry. These are individuals  who are working at lower level positions, those who are business owners,  and those considered “Expats.” The latter comes to the United States for  graduate education and with more frequency is returning to Brazil. This  is directly related to the growth of the Brazilian economy. 

It is also important to understand that Latino is not an accurate term  for individuals who live in the LatAm region. Individuals living in that   
6 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

region have a nationalistic identity based on the country in which they  reside. For instance, those living in Colombia are Colombians, those in  Peru are Peruvians, and so on. These countries compete among them selves and also have trade relationships with each other. They also have  distinct histories that have formed and shaped their cultures. However,  when people from LatAm immigrate to the United States many of these  differences tend to dissipate and a new culture emerges. Thus, they have  a shared set of experiences that are different from individuals who remain  in their native land, but more in common with individuals from other  LatAm countries now living in the United States. When these individuals  move to the United States, they are lumped together into one demo 

graphic (Latinos) with a coveted collective buying power that marketers  are trying to understand and capture. 

**A Brief History** 

The United States is a nation of immigrants. For the 237 plus years since  the nation’s founding, the population has grown by an influx of people from  other lands. Towards the end of the 19th and beginning of the 20th century,  European immigrants led the way. Although different immigrant groups  have peaked in that period, Latinos were always part of the growth equation. 

Mexican immigrants have the longest tenure in this country with  immigrants having a history that goes back to the founding of this coun try. This is due to the geographical proximity and the many territorial  wars that were fought. But this is beyond the scope of this book, as we  are working with the modern era beginning in the 20th century. The  initial wave of Latinos into the United States centered on major cities and  the Southwest: Mexicans in the Southwest and California; Puerto Ricans  and Cubans in New York City (NYC). The Castro era in the early 1960s  also saw the movement into the Miami area by Cubans and that city has  remained a hub for refugees, with a steady influx migrating to the island  and settling in the city. A spike in Cuban immigration occurred in 1980  when over 125,000 Cubans left the island with the encouragement of  the Castro regime. These individuals became known as the “Marielitos.”  Later, more immigrants from the Caribbean and South America flocked  to the area.  
Latinos Emerge 7 

Puerto Ricans have enjoyed a special relationship with the United  States in that they have been U.S. citizens since 1917\. Their migration to  the United States began in the 1920s and continued strongly through the  1960s. Beginning in the later part of the 1950s and through the 1970s, a  pattern of migration back to Puerto Rico began to take place mostly due  to “Operation Bootstrap,” a tax incentive based program to grow industry  in Puerto Rico. 

Under “Operation Bootstrap,” companies could set up manufactur ing facilities on the island and would not be required to pay taxes. This  helped grow Puerto Rico’s economy and educational system and this  resulted in many Puerto Ricans going back to the island. In the 1990s  the law was reversed and the Puerto Rican economy began to suffer as  many corporations began moving their manufacturing facilities to other  countries. Because of the ease with which Puerto Ricans can go to the  mainland, migration outside the island began again. This consistent out 

ward migration of a well-educated and bilingual workforce has led to  there being more Puerto Ricans living outside of the island than there  are currently living on it.4 This new generation of Puerto Rican migrants  brings with them science, technology, and engineering degrees as well as  a certain amount of management acumen and experience. It has been  called a “Brain Drain” that has benefited companies in the U.S. mainland. 

For most of the 20th century, Puerto Ricans in the mainland were  concentrated in NYC and the Northeast. A significant growth can be seen  in Central Florida in the last two decades. 

Immigrants from the Dominican Republic began to migrate to NYC  in the 1960s with a significant surge in the 1990s. Dominicans are mostly  in the Northeast, but like most Caribbean countries are well represented  in South Florida. With close to 1.5 million residents, they are the fifth  largest group of Latinos in the United States. Many of the next generation  children are beginning to emerge in the professional ranks. 

Beginning in 1980, immigration patterns took on a much different  shape showing a movement toward the North from South and Central  America, and the Caribbean. However, as we can see in Figure 1.1, Lati nos started spreading beyond traditional hubs. 

The Latino population is most highly represented in the states of  California, Texas, and Florida. These have always been strongholds for   
8 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

Latino immigrants. But now there are other states that have over a half a  million Hispanic residents. These are Arizona, Colorado, Georgia, Illinois,  Massachusetts, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Caro lina, Pennsylvania, Virginia, and Washington. Alabama had a 6.6% surge  in its Hispanic population between 2008 and 2009\. It is also important to  consider that the population of Latinos is on such a quick rise that in New  Mexico and California, the percentage of Latinos and Whites who live in  the state are equal. Texas will be the next to hit this milestone.

Latinos Emerge 9 

The elections of 2012 saw the emergence and importance of the  Latino voter. President Barrack Obama decidedly beat his opponent Mitt  Romney in this demographic by well over 40%. Many analyst and politi cal pundits believe that the elections could have turned out differently  had the Republican party taken a more inclusive tone toward Latinos and  not have alienated the group.5 This is an appropriate topic for debate,  but beyond the scope of this book. However, it did bring to the forefront  certain trends in the market that made companies reconsider how they  distribute their budgets. For instance, as the group has moved toward full  acculturation, there has been a movement in many corporations to place  the marketing budgets under the general category. Postelection, it appears  that many of these firms are now separating the line item for multicul 

tural markets in their budgets. Many Latino professional organizations,  such as the Hispanic Alliance for Career Enhancement (HACE), have  also reported a resurgence to recruit Latinos. This leads us to an impor tant innovation source—workforce development, and its impact on U.S.  competitiveness. The remainder of the chapters will cover multiple areas  of interest in developing a Latino Innovation Ecosystem. 

**The Shift in Demographics** 

As the United States transitions to a country of more diverse represen tation, companies have sought out strategies to recruit talent that is an  appropriate representation of the markets they serve and the communities  in which they operate. Creation of products and services that are market  sensitive has been a mantra for finding the best diverse talent available.  Essentially, D\&I has gone from a “nice to have” to a “good way to do  business” for many organizations. They have adjusted their hiring strate gies and policies with varying degrees of success to reflect a more inclusive  environment. But as mentioned previously, just hiring these individuals is  not enough. Diversity in itself does not provide a competitive advantage.  In many cases, these organizations have hired the talent and are asking  “now what?” This is where innovation, culture, globalization, and U.S.  competitiveness interact in helping build programs that help establish a  competitive advantage.  
10 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION **Summary**   
The United States has been the beneficiary of the great Latino immigra tion. Latinos are a diverse group that will continue to expand and have an  influence on U.S. culture and prosperity. The growth of this demographic  is expanding beyond traditional Latino hubs and must be considered in  future planning.  
**CHAPTER 2** 

**Beyond Diversity** 

To develop programs that lead to sustainable innovation success, you  need a workforce that is well prepared through skills and training. You  also need to provide an environment that will encourage an innovative  mindset. In this chapter, we discuss the challenges Latinos face in prepar 

ing to compete in an information- and knowledge-based economy that  places a high value on innovation. 

**Shaping the New Workforce** 

The shifting demographics of the American landscape show that there is  a movement toward a workforce that will be 31% of Latino descent by  2050\.1 This is significant because it is from where the United States will  derive much of its knowledge workers—the source of innovation. Shap 

ing this new workforce requires unlocking the innovative capabilities of the  Latino workforce and integrating Latinos into an innovation ecosystem that  is multi-industry and multi-functional. This ecosystem has multiple build ing blocks that include education, access to technology, and improving the  standard of living for Latinos. Each of these topics is addressed in regard to  how they impact Latino innovation development. It is important to under stand that these are major contributors to an overall innovation ecosystem  

that feeds the Business Innovation Ecosystem (BIE) in Figure 2.1. The BIE is a framework concept deployed by the Global Targeting  Corporation to describe a subset of a national innovation ecosystem. It  takes a strategic view of establishing a sustained innovation infrastructure  that begins by understanding how its people view and define innovation.  Since corporations are made up of individuals from diverse backgrounds,  they view, interpret, and accept innovation in different ways. Once indi vidual perceptions of innovation are defined, they can be aligned and  innovation processes such as ENOVALE™, a Global Targeting proprietary   
12 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION ![][image4]***Figure 2.1 Business innovation ecosystem***

methodology, can be implemented; then technology can be applied to  enable this infrastructure. The People, Process, and Technology elements  of the BIE are predominantly internal elements. The other two compo nents extend to the organization’s customer base and then to their cus tomers as well, thus forming an Extended Enterprise. 

**Developing the New Workforce** 

The development of the Latino workforce will require a concerted effort  from businesses, government, and Latinos themselves to ensure future  innovation success. These are all elements of a national innovation ecosys tem. To begin, let’s understand how Hispanic households are performing.  As of 2010, the median household income was \$37,759 and the poverty  level from 2009 to 2010 went from 25.3% to 26.6%.2 This is certainly  not going in the right direction, and as we will see shortly, when coupled  with educational attainment it causes some concern. 

This particular demographic has challenges in terms of education pre paredness, inclusion into the work environment, and growth patterns.    
Beyond Diversity 13 

Education and attained skills correlate with what one needs to compete  for a job and then be productive in it. When considering how to best  leverage the innovative capabilities of a multicultural workforce, one must  consider the Barriers and Accelerators of innovation. 

It is important to spend a little time defining the Barriers and Accel erators concept from an innovation perspective: 

• Barriers are the obstacles that organizations face in trying  to implement sustainable innovation success. They can take  many different forms and can be unique to different organi zations or demographic groups. By minimizing or eliminat ing them, an organization can have a defined path toward  sustainable innovation success. Common Barriers are Lead ership Style, Communication Effectiveness, and Employee  Involvement. 

• Accelerators are those things that enable organizations to  reach innovation goals quicker. The term “thing” is used  loosely because it can apply to processes, procedures, environ ment, leadership, or many other things that could be unique  to an organization. 

We will look at the most important Accelerator first. In our opinion,  that is education and training. Education certainly provides individuals  with the tools for enabling innovation, because it provides a source to  develop critical thinking skills, context, and allows individuals the capa 

bilities to analyze, synthesize, and evaluate knowledge to generate new  ideas. Consequently, Latinos are facing Barriers in educational attain ment. This can be seen when comparing graduation rates with those of  other groups in Table 2.1. 

Innovation is dependent on improving access to tools and using them  correctly. Education and training provide the link for using these tools  appropriately. It is also the vehicle for allowing Latinos to leave the realm  of lower poverty levels by providing individuals with employment attain 

ing skills. Poverty levels actually trended in the wrong direction from  2009 to 2010 having gone from 25.3% to 26.6% for all major ethnic  groups.
