Education and poverty levels have an impact on innovation, because  they provide a means for accessing and using technology and data. In  terms of U.S. growth areas, innovation is critical for facilitating growth in  technology, healthcare, and analytics (Big Data). Although it is important  to know how a certain group defines innovation, it is also important to  have the skills to apply it into an innovative venture. 

Education is the key to guiding a Latino workforce to achieve its  innovative potential. It is a portal that leads to the development of critical  thinking skills. This is an effort that must begin at a very early age, accord ing to Sylvia Puente, Executive Director of the Latino Policy Forum, a  Chicago-based organization that facilitates the involvement of Latinos at  all levels of public decision-making. They seek to inform, influence, and  develop leadership through various programs. To develop leaders “in the  masses that we need, we must invest in early education,” according to Ms.  Puente. Her organization is an advocate and promoter of the “Abriendo  Puertas” program that encourages parents to read to children early on.  These are the kind of programs that are vital to ensure early education  success and eventually success in the workforce. It is critical in developing  an innovation ecosystem to integrate and fund these programs. 

The current state of Latino education is challenged by a combination of  factors that are identified in Pew Research study on Hispanic educational  attainment. This study, conducted in 2009 (and updated in 2012), found  that the lower educational attainment by Latinos is due to four factors: 

• Lack of funding for education 

• Poor English skills   
Beyond Diversity 15 

• Youth bored with school 

• Don’t see education as a means to securing a job 

The Pew study3 is interesting in that its findings appear to touch upon  areas that seem to be cultural and generational in nature. Many young  Latinos are molded by their parent’s belief that just getting a job and  working hard at it is sufficient for success. This is mostly associated with  Latinos who are either not acculturated or fully acculturated. There is  something missing from the results. The experience for these individuals  is varied from the social economic perspective. It can also be due to finan cial reality. It tends to reside in labor and tangibles. 

In developing a more in-depth understanding of educational attain ment for Latinos we see patterns that are beginning to trend in the right  direction in some areas. For instance, Pew updated research found that in  2012, 69% of Latino high school graduates entered college. This is sig nificantly up from recent years, but still requires some attention to ensure  continuation. The challenge is to now ensure higher graduation rates. For  instance, as of 2010 Latinos 25 and older had a bachelor’s degree and of  that 1.1% attained a master’s or higher. Considering that as a percentage  of the total population of Latinos, the results are poor. Also, consider ing that as a percentage of other groups such as Asians, the number is  abysmal. Latinos may make up 15% of the population, but they are only  6.2% of the total full-time college students enrolled in 2010\.4 Could this  be attributed to the four factors mentioned here, and if so, how do we fix  it? Mentorship and professional networking are viable options. 

In concluding this section, we realize that as a nation we must con tinue to push for funding programs that emphasize early education, since  currently 23.2% of all elementary and high school students are Latinos.5 We must also emphasize mentorship and encouragement to have this  population to first graduate and then succeed in the professional world. 

**The Corporate World** 

As Latinos begin to occupy positions in greater numbers in corporations;  they are also emerging in roles that impact corporate operations. The  growth of Latinos is significant, but almost 32% of this population is still   
16 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

not in the civilian workforce. When we look at Latinos in the workforce  who are in management, sciences, and business roles, it is only at 19%.6 Keeping our focus on corporations we see that they can range from small  to medium-sized ventures to Fortune 500 enterprises. Innovation is not  limited to large technology firms, and it is not the exclusive domain of  companies that manufacture tangible products. Innovation in services is a  major point of emphasis for many companies. 

Corporate America continues to rely on global growth and innovation.  The companies that have had the most success in producing innovation  can trace their success to that of providing their human capital with  resources and processes that leverage their talents. They provide them  with mentors, infrastructure, and processes that accelerate the develop 

ment of innovative talents as well as with the knowledge to think criti cally. These successful companies seek and develop talent and in the case  of the largest firms they also make a concerted effort to develop a diverse  and well-trained talent base. This is generally an individual company  effort rather than a concerted effort by the United States as a nation. The  bottom line is that corporations will promote their best talent regardless  of background. Latinos must become assertive in this respect. But there  are certain things that corporations can do to make the most out of the  Latino talent they have, according to Murray Mann of Global Diversity  Solutions. 

As a diversity consultant to Fortune 500 companies, Murray has  found that the firms that have maximized their Latino talent have done it  by addressing four key challenges in recruiting Latino talent. These chal lenges are as follows: 

• Lack of cultural competence by hiring managers. Many work ers also don’t have enough of a comfort level in expressing  themselves to their own managers. Often, Latino talent can  ease the communications barrier as well. 

• Screening out the very talent they are looking for. Many  times a corporation decides to use a computer-generated list  of candidates rather than interviewing individuals who may  possess more talent and capability. By taking this approach  these companies eliminate the very talent they seek.  
Beyond Diversity 17 

• Minimizing “Micro-inequality”: Intangible things people  don’t see, like accent, but affect their overall judgment of  individuals. 

• Lack of long-term mentorship—to prepare individuals for  roles when they are not the obvious roles. This is especially  true in that “Latinos are recruited for diversity, but rewarded  for performance,” as per Murray Mann. Consequently, many  are in positions as the head of diversity more as a company  representative, rather than taking positions responsible for  profit and loss (P\&L) and leading the activities that lead to  innovation. 

As you will discover later in this book, the Latino population has a  great influence on the consumer marketing efforts of many corporations.  But what influence do they exert in the workplace? Given the growth of  this particular population, one would assume that their representation in  the workplace would be reflective of the growing buying power. Is this the  case? Why or why not? 

First, we need to analyze the multigenerational landscape that cur rently exists in organizations today, and then discern if other factors, such  as culture and heredity exert a degree of influence as well. In many organ izations, three generational segments interact in the workplace: Baby  Boomers, Generation X, and Millennials. For definition purposes, Baby  Boomers are those born between 1946 and 1964, Generation X were  born between 1965 and 1979, and Millennials were born after 1979\. In  addition to the life-cycle segments outlined here, the global marketplace  also integrates cultural differences into each generational segment, which  adds a level of complexity to organizational success. Cultural and genera tional differences do impact Latinos in the workplace. It is important to  remember the rapidly growing American born second-generation Latinos  will also require leaders to consider rates of acculturation and assimila tion, the hybridization of both, and to what degree each affects Latinos’  success in the workplace. These divergent cultural processes do have an  impact on innovation. 

Two concepts that require clarification are acculturation and assimila tion. Acculturation is the process of adapting to the traits of the majority   
18 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

culture, while also being immersed in the values, beliefs, practices, and  traditions of one’s own culture, which are maintained. Alternately, assimi lation is an adoption of the host culture’s traits, with some abandonment  of the tenets of one’s original ethnic culture. Given the sheer number of  Latinos in the workforce, it is important to understand how this group  is acculturating and how it is being represented in corporate America.  However, this group is underrepresented in leadership roles. Since Lati nos represent a growing consumer market, it would make sense that they  

should be recruited and mentored into positions of greater influence. Developing a pipeline into corporate, education, and governmental  positions starts with preparation. We do this through the skills we acquire  through education and experience. Additionally, you have to know where  to look to find the right opportunities in corporations. There are many  organizations that do take an active role in matching Latino talent with  corporations and then nurturing relationships to provide Latinos a path  to success as they overcome cultural barriers and are able to apply them selves accordingly. HACE is one of those organizations that have proven  its capacity to help many Latinos. In fact, one of the authors, Vinny, is a  good example. 

Having served as a U.S. Army Aviator, Vinny spent numerous years in  the service and was ready to leave and pursue a career in the private sector.  It was a career fair in Chicago that led him to attain a position with IBM  after having received his MBA. He later went on to serve as the Chairman  of HACE to continue its mission. 

Just attaining the first position is not enough. Early in a Latino profes sional’s career there should be opportunities for someone to find a mentor  who has faced similar challenges, as well as building a diverse network  of other professionals. Although some organizations provide mentorship  opportunities, the issue of innovation is still not addressed and nurtured. 

**The Importance of Mentorship** 

As found in business research and literature, networking has always been  the buzzword since any of us embarked on our first professional foray  into the world of work. Most if not all of us have had varying degrees  of success following the advice of our professional sages, and some of us   
Beyond Diversity 19 

have been fortunate enough to identify a more formalized version of a  sage—a mentor. 

Mentors by and large are very difficult to find, and it is even more  difficult to identify one who truly is an influencer in the organization,  industry, or both to which they are affiliated. This is becoming a more  complicated undertaking, given the instability of careers in the corpo 

rate world of today; great influencers are often poached by other organi zations that are in dire need of visionaries and strategists to “right the  ship,” and create a new plan for the future of their companies. With these  leaders no longer in the fold, how will the next generation assert their  influence on innovation teams so that they, too, may serve as mentors of  the future? With the challenges in identifying and securing a mutually  beneficial mentor–protégé dynamic, companies must also consider that  Latinos have specific challenges that differ from their Anglo counterparts  in achieving upward mobility. One we mentioned previously is Micro 

inequalities, and sometimes it is a matter of feeling comfortable with the  groups in which they interact. 

Throughout recent history, the challenges of underrepresented minor ity groups in the workforce have been somewhat mitigated by corporate  policies, government regulation and the like, and more formalized men toring processes and programs. Yet, Latinos have not achieved the same  level of representation at the highest echelons of organizational leader ship. Perhaps due to sheer strength in numbers, this seems to be chang ing, although challenges still exist. Given that Latinos are still working  toward equal representation, is there a disconnect somewhere in the men toring process that hinders their progress? We are certainly not suggesting  that Latinos do not have mentoring skills; it is more an issue of Latinos  not having the level of influence within their organizations to develop  another generation for succession planning. 

Although not essential, mentor–protégé relationships are often more  successful depending on the level of similarity the participants have with  one another, whether from a cultural, linguistic, or value-driven dynamic.  This stands to reason of course; the more we identify with another person,  the more likely we are to support those who are reflections of how we see  ourselves. We’ve often heard the phrase “you remind me of me when I was  your age”; in a workplace environment, a mentor who envisions a young   
20 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

protégé as someone who may follow the same professional development  course as themselves would be more likely to share their wisdom and  experiences with the said protégé. This relationship provides both psycho social and emotional support, as well as career guidance. However, if the  protégé does not perform to expectations, the mentor could experience a  negative impact to their career. 

Given the efforts Latinos have expended to achieve leadership roles  within organizations, a Latino mentor with great knowledge and skill may  be hesitant to cultivate a mentorship arrangement, as they themselves are  working toward acceptance at the higher ranks. They may resist undertak 

ing such a level or responsibility, as unanticipated shortcomings by their  protégé may derail their own professional path. Given the unavailabil ity of representation, this may be too high a risk for not only their own  future, but given the collective nature of the Latino culture, they may feel  obligated to their heritage to successfully navigate their own path toward  success. We have seen this take shape as many Latino corporate leaders  are actively engaged in Latino affinity groups early in their career, but lose  contact and commitment after arriving at the Director level. We had the  opportunity to speak to Lou Nieto, a successful Latino who has always  maintained a close mentorship relationship with Latino professionals. 

Lou has served at the pinnacle of corporate America having served as  a divisional president and corporate board member for several Fortune  500 corporations. He has set an example by remaining actively involved  in professional development groups (PDGs) regardless of his professional  corporate positions. He credits this to a supportive family environment  and attending schools with great support. This collective view also tran 

scends into innovation because he has always believed that innovation is  not limited to one department. Instead, it is generated from all parts of  the business. 

Has the advent of social networking sites such as LinkedIn and pro fessional development and networking organizations undermined the  proven groundwork of cultivating mentors through carefully crafted rela tionships? Is it possible to develop a professional relationship virtually?  Do we know if the availability of these options has enabled us to cast a  wider net from which to build our networking base? With face-to-face  encounters less important, we believe it has resulted in the growth and   
Beyond Diversity 21 

dependence on technology by this generation, resulting in the need to  develop new strategies. 

**The Power of Professional Networking Groups** 

In the world of innovation, there are multiple groups that exist to share  best practices with each other in a collaborative manner. The collaborators  are not necessarily oriented to working on specific projects, but instead on  sharing specific techniques or successes they have had. This is referred to  as “open innovation,” and it has its roots in technology and research and  development (R\&D). The members of these forums collaborate across  industries and geographies. They promulgate the idea that firms can ben efit from using external practices. There are also open innovation forums  that are proprietary in nature because they belong to corporations. What  they all have in common is that they share processes and success sto 

ries. This permits innovation to move beyond products. You can now  apply innovation in services and you can go beyond the technology realm  in innovation. This is where professional development and networking  groups can add value to their membership. 

The Latino community does not have any organizations dedicated  to innovation, as in open forums. However, organizations exist that can  potentially be more powerful in harnessing the innovative capabilities of  Latinos. These are known as professional development groups (PDGs),  and their business is to develop human potential. All innovation ema 

nates from human beings; people define innovation differently and by  capturing this energy, talent, and attitude you can align your organization  for innovation success. PDGs are uniquely positioned for this, but have  not been able to leverage this beyond D\&I initiatives. Now is the time to  answer the “now what” of D\&I discussed in Chapter 1\. 

PDGs are organizations that provide a platform for Latinos to net work with other individuals in the same profession. These groups pro vide significant value because they offer opportunities to improve certain  skills, but more importantly they provide an access to corporations and  other organizations. PDGs serve as excellent repositories of intellectual  capital and a means for identifying talent. Much of the research that was  done for Project Impact was conducted through the members of these   
22 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

groups. The multi-disciplinary background served as an excellent basis  for capturing opinions that were common to a culture rather than to a  particular industry. 

The PDGs go beyond the groups that are advocates for housing,  immigration, and the acquisition of basic skills. PDGs are the natural  extension of these basic groups. PDGs are also sources of mentorship for  these organizations. We will discuss some of the more prominent groups  and their mission statements. 

Dr. Caraballo interviewed some of the leadership of these organiza tions to gain some insight and perspective on professional development  and innovation. Their input is valuable because each of their organiza tions interacts with communities, educational institutions, governmental  entities, and global corporations. They are also important in providing  mentoring opportunities. These organizations focus on the professional  development of the individual, similar to Global Targeting’s ENOVALE™  Framework that begins with the belief that all innovation begins with the  individual. Thus, our shared value is that we focus on the human element. 

**Association of Latino Professionals in Finance and  Accounting (ALPFA)** 

An organization that exhibits innovation through change, ALPFA7 has  gone from serving Latinos in the financial field to one that serves a  broader constituency with a mission to develop Latino business profes sionals. Through their 41 professional and 120 student chapters, they  are leading the way to develop the innovative capabilities of Latino  professionals. 

We had the opportunity to speak to the leadership of ALPFA to  understand how their approach to “Building Latino Leaders” can lead  to innovation success. The Vice President for Programs, Sandra Sanchez  Pierre, of this organization believes that their approach through confer 

ences and developing employee resource groups (ERGs) provides Latinos  with forums to express themselves, “Without scrutiny you can be proud  of your Latinismo,” according to Ms. Sanchez. This is valuable insight  into our own research shows that Latinos and women in particular tend  to not express themselves in the workplace, because they believe their   
Beyond Diversity 23 

ideas may not be given serious consideration. This is certainly considered  a barrier to innovation: the perception that ideas are not valid. Many of  the programs this organization provides can address this issue. 

The research purpose of Global Targeting’s Project Impact study is  to understand attitudes, opinions, and disposition of different cultures  toward innovation. Our conversations with ALPFA added several other  dimensions to consider in understanding how culture impacts innovation. 

Zenaida Mendoza, the Chief Creative Officer for ALPFA, also dis cussed that generations communicate differently and through different  media and technology. Therefore, in trying to establish innovation pro grams with Latino knowledge workers, corporations should consider how  to deliver programs that resonate with this demographic. 

Pamela Ravare Brown, ALPFA’s Chief Operating Officer, has taken  this a step further by realizing how important it is to understand the cog nitive aspect associated with innovation from a leadership perspective. In  preparing Latinos to assume leadership positions in the next 10–15 years,  ALPFA realizes that identifying drivers of innovation is important to the  next generation. Their leadership programs emphasize critical thinking  that allows these emerging leaders to adapt, adopt, and become conduits  of innovation in their organizations. 

ALPFA clearly has a defined plan to empower the Latino leaders  of tomorrow by providing networking and training opportunities. The  organization is a conduit into the corporate world for Latinos, and it  adds value to its members because its operation has innovation embed 

ded into it. 

**Hispanic Alliance for Career Enhancement (HACE)** 

Since it was founded in 1982, HACE8 has empowered high potential  Latinos by helping these individuals advance, develop, and promote  Latino professionals all across the country. The mission of HACE is to  positively impact the American workplace by cultivating the pipeline of  Latino talent and providing Latino professionals the insight, access, and  support to be successful in their careers. 

HACE facilitates the transition of individuals into the workforce  by emphasizing mentorship that begins in high school and continues   
24 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

through mid-career levels. Patricia Mota, the organization’s Senior Direc tor of Community Outreach, believes that HACE’s value comes from 

• making cultural connections for first-generation Latinos; • providing education in cultural relevancy and how to succeed  in the workplace; 

• leveraging Latino culture for success. 

They offer professional development opportunities that help develop high  potential individuals through “Mujeres de HACE,” a leadership program  designed exclusively for women. This is an excellent program to encour age innovation efforts, and ties in directly to one of the most important  barriers to innovation from our Project Impact study. 

In our research, we asked one question to gauge how well an indi vidual is comfortable in asserting their ideas in the workplace. We asked  survey respondents, “Do you not bring up ideas in the workplace because  you are afraid to be ridiculed?” Women answered this question in the  affirmative significantly more than men. It is our opinion that providing  programs like HACE’s “Mujeres” will provide women with a sense of  empowerment and provide them with confidence so that they can bring  up the ideas that will lead to innovative environments. 

HACE also helps high performing individuals to develop their lead ership skills by teaching team leadership techniques in its “Leadership  Academy.” In each of these programs, Latinos find their strengths and  how to communicate them through a self-discovery process. These kinds  of programs are ones all corporations should leverage and are also ideal for  innovation enhancement. 

**National Association of Hispanic MBAs (NSHMBA)** 

The National Association of Hispanic MBAs9 sits at the pinnacle of  Latino PDGs. The organization has four clearly defined objectives as part  of its strategic plan: 

• To increase the number of Hispanics graduating from master’s  business degree programs through scholarships, professional  development, and mentorship  
Beyond Diversity 25 

• To enhance career management opportunities for Hispanic  MBAs from school to leadership positions, through job place ment and world-class professional development 

• To be the partner of choice for organizations seeking to hire  and develop Hispanic talent 

• To recruit and retain as lifelong members a majority of His panic MBAs 

Manny Gonzalez is NSHMBA’s CEO, and he believes as Latinos con tinue to assume positions of leadership in the corporate world they will  have a more prominent role in developing innovation successes at many  corporations. In his view, innovation is about programs that impact effi ciency and effectiveness. Introducing the “Chaos Factor” into daily opera tions is a way of adding value to many organizations. It is his belief that  Latinos do face challenges in implementing innovation in corporations.  He mentions three Barriers to innovation that Latinos must overcome: 

• Culture—Corporations are driven by “Wall Street” culture  and Latinos have not had much exposure to this way of  thinking. Consequently, it creates a certain amount of fear for  Latinos in corporations; however, this “Fear Factor” should  diminish as Latinos reach critical mass in companies. The pro grams NSHMBA provides help Latinos adjust to the corpo rate environment and provide corporations with information  to help them become more sensitive to the Latino workforce.  The NSHMBA programs bridge gaps through networking  and relationship building opportunities. 

• Engagement—Lack of understanding of Latino culture leads  to a lack of engaging professionals in innovation efforts.  “Since I don’t understand you, I don’t engage you,” seems  to be a common encounter expressed by NSHMBA mem bers, according to Mr. Gonzalez. To overcome this Barrier,  NSHMBA leverages its relationships with its corporate  partners through ERGs. ERGs are internally organized corpo rate affiliations of employees with a purpose of representing  Latinos. The visibility and importance of these groups has   
26 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

recently been elevated because they are now being organized  strategically to align with business unit objectives. 

• Competitiveness—Many Latinos don’t have the opportunity  to attend top tier graduate schools. This may lead to Latinos  being misaligned in the recruiting process for positions in cor porate America. Often these are the positions that are pivotal  in developing innovation practices. To help Latinos overcome  this Barrier, NSHMBA provides programs to help Latinos  identify the right graduate program and how to prepare a  competitive application. 

Mr. Gonzalez believes that the work of NSHMBA, through its 39  chapters, contributes to the development of the Latino Innovation Eco system by creating knowledge platforms to collapse some of the Barriers  Latinos face. 

**Summary** 

Latinos will be the largest part of the future U.S. workforce. To prepare  for future innovative success, considerable investment will have to be  made in education and mentorship. PDGs are important for early educa tion, training, and networking opportunities.  
**CHAPTER 3** 

**The Latino Influence on  the U.S. Economy** 

Innovation is a combination of ideas, techniques, or both that can create  new value for customers. For an innovation to be accepted in the business  world, it must have a market. The Latino market provides an outlet for  innovative products and services, as well as a space for the training and  development of innovative skills. In this chapter, we present an overview  of the Latino market in the United States. 

**The Marketing Influence** 

The size and potential of the Latino market presents a compelling case for  marketers to develop products and services that will meet the demands of  this demographic. The industries that most target Latinos are consumer  packaged goods, media, and automotive, as per the Association of His 

panic Advertising Agencies (AHAA). Although much of the attention has  been in selling to the market, not much emphasis has been placed on how  leveraging the innovative capabilities of this workforce can generate addi tional sales for the segment, as well as providing innovations that cross  over into other disciplines and services. 

In marketing to Latinos, many advertising agencies have for years  taken the position that you cannot market to the Latino market as one big  generic segment. That may have been the case for many years (and it still  remains this way), as immigrants were slowly coming from their native  lands and were familiar with certain brands. As we focus more on genera 

tions, consumers from the Latino market seem to have acculturated faster.  Inter-racial marriages are seen more often now, and this brings with it a  certain amount of exposure and acceptance of other brands. Also, we live  in a technology-driven world, where many immigrants coming to this   
28 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

country have been exposed to some of the American products already in  their native lands. It may be cliché, but we do live in a global commu nity. It is becoming clear that generational influences are becoming more  important than geographical lineage in marketing. 

Let’s start with a general market example. Suppose the marketing  group of a consumer products company decided to target young male  professionals in their 20s and very early 30s. Suppose the product that  they are selling is an energy drink. Now there are many energy drinks  on the market these days, so how would one differentiate this product?  Using the above information, we know from our research that we detail in  Chapter 5, that this particular group has one distinguishing characteristic  in that innovation is most meaningful to them when it combines both  elements of improvement and change. 

In order to market energy drinks to this group, one would need to do  one of two things. (We realize specific market research is also needed.)  First, the drink would need to significantly outperform its competitors  and second, it would need to address more than existing needs. Remem 

ber that this type of product is widely used meaning that individuals  have both experience and knowledge of the product. This brings an addi tional dimension of difficulty in increasing purchase behavior. One could  increase sales without making any claims to the product being innovative.  But then, the product would not be a challenge or threaten its competi tion. Therefore, one solution could be to increase the time that the prod uct lasts in the individual’s bloodstream, thereby increasing performance.  Or, there could be an additional need, want, or desire that the product  would address. One approach could be a time-release mechanism so that  the product delivers the same energy boost throughout its life cycle. This  example is strictly based on product attributes. Of course, there are other  elements of the marketing mix to consider, especially in communications. 

Consider the same group; how could one use the concept of inno vation that focuses on new perspectives for this particular demographic  group? When dealing with a new product, service, or technology, we are  dealing with needs that are yet unmet or potentially unfulfilled. It can also  be a want or a desire. What this means is that the needs have not yet been  established and there is little or no knowledge and experience with the  particular product, service, or technology. The key to increasing purchase   
 The Latino Influence on the U.S. Economy 29 

behavior for this group is to understand what needs are unmet and unful filled, understanding the desires of the group, or understanding what  makes them want something. If that is too difficult or time-consuming  or too expensive, then one can always use increased performance as a  method of identifying innovation. 

Performance, however, may not be able to provide an effective com petitive advantage. It is best with new products to highlight the need that  is unmet or unfulfilled. For instance, the iPad essentially filled the need  for a lightweight tablet-like computer without the extraneous hardware  but with good sound and excellent screen quality. In reality, the iPad is  not a computer, or a cell phone, but it meets a set of needs as well as  unfulfilled needs, just making it more convenient to users. It meets the  needs for lightweight, accessibility, and portable information acquisition;  and it also meets the need of a true new (unique) high-tech product that  other manufacturers do not provide. 

If one wanted to reach generation X Latinos, whether male or female,  the emphasis would be on the fact that the object is better, that is, it  improved meeting either unmet needs or meeting needs that exist but  with exceptional performance. But it also requires a deep understanding  of consumer behavior to determine the features that would best sell this  product. This is a good example to describe how the object must trans 

form itself to be classified as innovative. Many products are transformed  over their entire life cycle, but how often are these transformations inno vative? They are innovative when the individual with their knowledge and  experience perceives or understands the benefit, given that their needs,  wants, and desires are being better met, and that performance exceeds  what is existing in the marketplace. 

In Chapter 5, we present data analyses to help you understand the  concept of innovation from the perspective of Global Targeting. Just  because something is new does not in fact make it an innovation. We are  inundated with new products every day which are not innovative but in  fact do fulfill a need. We are not talking about those objects or products;  instead, we are talking about those that are perceived or understood or  even accepted as innovative. But the Latino market is large and growing;  it is important to understand this market because it represents opportuni ties to apply innovation to products and services designed for the market.  
30 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION **Latino Consumers and Innovation**   
Latinos represent approximately 17% of the total U.S. population, num bering approximately 50 million (the majority of whom are of Mexican  origin); they wield \$1.3 trillion in buying power, and are geographically  very easy to reach, as their populations are concentrated primarily in four  U.S. states: California, Texas, New York, and Florida. But as we saw in  Figure 1.1, this is shifting a bit. Some firms have succeeded in penetrating  the psyche of these consumers, while other businesses have not. Inter estingly, most advertisers only allocate less than 1% of their budgets to  deliberate Hispanic targeted messages. For a population segment that has  grown 43% in the 10-year period from 2000 to 2010 (the last census data  available), and by all indications will continue to do so, why are compa 

nies not investing more, or being more effective in their campaigns? One of the challenges associated with communicating with this seg ment effectively is that it is diverse. Although there has been some transi tion, this significant population still has many who identify themselves by  their country of origin, not the umbrella terms of “Hispanic” or “Latino.”  For instance, you ask someone of Hispanic origin where they are from,  and almost never do they say “South America,” “Central America,” or  “Latin America.” They say, “I am from Puerto Rico,” or “I am from  Mexico, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador,” and so on. It’s really not too much  different from someone who was born and raised in the United States;  meeting new people in any social gathering will inevitably lead to the  question, “Where are you from?” Respondents will usually answer with  their current state of residence, but may qualify their answer by identify ing their birthplace, if different. For example, a conversation with some one whom you’ve never met may evolve from “Where are you from?” to  “I live in Texas, but I was born in New Jersey” or some derivation of this  interaction. When travelling abroad however, we are often labeled as just  “Americans,” with our country of origin being determined by our mode of  dress, our language, our mannerisms, and so forth. Unless asked, the term  “American” seems to serve as a descriptive enough label to anyone outside  the United States, thus assuming North America constitutes “America.”  In this example, are companies outside the United States already dis tinguishing the North American marketplace as distinctly “American,”   
 The Latino Influence on the U.S. Economy 31 

and by doing so, already identifying South America as a distinctly dif ferent marketplace? If European or Asian companies wanted to sell their  products in the United States, would they be effective in generalizing our  needs and wants as one big homogenous consumer group? Probably not\!  

Therefore, we should look at the Latino market in the same manner. To successfully navigate the Latino market, marketers must under stand the nuances of the many countries of origin that comprise these  Americans as those who have varied backgrounds, as well as some shared  aspects of cultural homogeneity. For example, a grocery store in one  county that serves the Hispanic community in that neighborhood may  sell different items than the grocery store serving the Latino population  in the next county, depending on the concentration of residents from a  particular country of origin. Another example is in the entertainment  industry. An artist’s popularity is often dependent upon the region of the  country that identifies with their type of talent. 

It is also important to consider generational trends as well; the Pew  Hispanic Center has found that 61% first-generation Latinos who reside  in the United States are more proficient in Spanish than English, but by  the third generation, this falls to 2%. Overwhelmingly, Latinos believe that  future generations must maintain their Spanish language skills, but also  accept the fact that proficiency in English is essential to achieve success. 

There are many examples of how companies re-strategized their mar keting approaches to be more sensitive to this particular population; not  with new products, but a more globally relatable message to encourage  new users (Latinos) to purchase products or services they may have never  considered previously. Let’s review a few examples: Taco Bell and Darden  Restaurants. 

Many of us may remember the iconic Chihuahua in previous Taco  Bell commercials, with the tag line “Yo quiero Taco Bell” (I want Taco  Bell). Although long running and attention generating, the ad was con sidered degrading to Hispanics, and Taco Bell pulled the ad. In 2012,  they rebounded with the now running “Live Mas” to appeal to a broader  audience base by adopting the idea of Hispanics/Latinos being American  with different cultural backgrounds. 

Darden Restaurants, owners of Olive Garden, Red Lobster, and  Denny’s Restaurants, have also engaged the Latino market by using   
32 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

authentic representatives of the population who have crossover appeal.  Since 25% of Denny’s customer base is Latino, they have profiled Cesar  Milan, popular star of the TV show “The Dog Whisperer” in a series of  online videos, as he possesses this necessary crossover appeal for all cul 

tural groups, but is authentically Latino. This also reflects some interest ing findings regarding Latino media patterns; there is a preference for TV  and the Web to newspapers, and Latinos are very active on social media.  Latinos don’t just virtually “window-shop” on mobile devices, they com plete their entire purchase process via these devices, utilizing QR codes,  navigational tools, and texting to interact with brands to lead them to  their purchase decisions. From the available research, this may be due to  the dominant youth demographic associated with the Latino population. 

Acculturation and assimilation are important concepts in marketing  because they have significant impact on the effectiveness of marketing  messages on target markets. Generational differences within specified  groups can also highlight consumer behavior patterns. When marketers  know this, they can create for themselves a competitive advantage versus  those that view the Latino market as unicultural. 

Although there are as many as 20 different cultures under the Latino  umbrella, if not more, there are some cultural commonalities that also  unify this market. 

The Latino market is considered “collectivist” in its value systems,  that is, society centric and interpersonal.1 No matter which generation  they identify with or belong to, there are ties that bind Latinos to each  other. Most Latinos desire to honor their heritage in some way, whether  it is through language or traditions, regardless of the degree to which  each member individually assimilates or acculturates into the dominant  culture. 

Another commonly identified trait that traverses all generations is the  respect for family, to include extended family and friends.2 Adherence to  group mores offers a sense of protection by the group, which is passed  down from generation to generation. Families normally operate under  a patriarchal pattern. The family will support the choices and decisions  made by the dominant male family member, and this often manifests in  extreme brand loyalty, as honoring the buying patterns of previous gen erations represents loyalty to the cultural group. This is a great challenge   
 The Latino Influence on the U.S. Economy 33 

for marketers, as the U.S. market is much more individualistic in orienta tion, and as has been alluded to, the trend toward more assimilation of  the Latino population into the U.S. culture complicates the approach  taken to communicate effectively. How do advertisers break the pattern of  brand loyalty to introduce new products and services while capturing the  cultural expectations that have been protected and preserved throughout  

the generations? Innovation opportunities may be the key here. Latino Baby Boomers, Generation X, and Millennials exhibit unique  life stage behaviors. As mentioned earlier, the Hispanic market is demo graphically very young; 20% of the population would be categorized as  Millennials. They represent 20% of all Millennials in the United States  totaling 51.7 million. They also represent almost 18 % of the Latin  American population—almost 100 million in number. A recent AHAA  study revealed that this segment exhibits cultural duality more than other  Hispanic generational groups, that is, they have a higher Anglo cultural  orientation than other Hispanic age groups. Is this due to their profi ciency with technology and social media? Does the availability of infor mation through these various media outlets expose them to the Anglo  lifestyle to such a degree that they begin to adopt aspects of the culture?  These are all great questions. They are very adept at researching informa tion and expect the information to be available to them when and where  they need it. As mentioned earlier, Latinos tend to use social media and  technology not only to conduct research prior to purchase but also to use  the technology to actually complete the purchase process. This will be  discussed in greater detail later in the book.  

Latino Gen Xers, numbering 19 million, are a significant target market,  and exhibit a proficiency with technology much like their Millennial gen erational neighbors, but with more disposable income to spend on more  sophisticated technology. This population continues to grow robustly. 

Latino Boomers represent 11% of the 81 million total Baby Boomers  residing in the United States currently. This generation, not surprisingly,  maintains the highest attachment to their culture, but exhibits many sim ilarities to their Anglo Boomers, for example, preservation of health and  wealth through investments and insurance. So how can marketers make  sense of all these competing influences? An understanding of the depth  of assimilation and acculturation of the Latino community is essential.  
34 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

Acculturation has been defined in many ways, but most simply, it  is the level of acceptance of the dominant culture in which one finds  oneself, without abandoning one’s culture of heritage. There is room for  adaptation, as situations dictate. Every culture and every generational  group has experienced acculturation to some degree. We transition from  high school to college, college to the working world, single to married,  move from job to job, state to state, and so forth, all life experiences  which require some degree of adjustment on our part to fit in with our  new environments. 

As Latinos migrate to new countries, states, or even neighborhoods,  there may be differences in buying choices; what they may have been  comfortable purchasing previously may no longer be available, and they  must move from what was to what is as their new reality. This may present  opportunities for marketers to challenge the brand loyalty Latinos his 

torically adhere to and introduce new products and services, especially to  those generations who are more technically adept, as they have a greater  exposure to new information, innovation, or knowledge management.  Therefore, since a very large segment of the Latino population tends to  be younger (and many second-generation family members are American  born), these youthful members are much more dependent on social media  and mobile devices to determine their purchasing decisions and behavior.  Perhaps this presents a greater potential for marketers to introduce new  products and services, and not be hampered by trying to break through  traditional buying patterns passed down through generations, as this tar get may eventually be considered bicultural. 

Assimilation on the other hand is a bit more dramatic from a cultural  maintenance perspective. There is an adoption of host cultural tenets,  with some loss of the ethnic identification to one’s heritage. There is evi dence that acculturation and assimilation patterns do have an impact on  the type of media Latinos rely on to dictate buying behaviors. From an  advertising perspective, this information can be very useful when craft ing identifiable messages and images, and there is a developing trend to  further segment Latino markets by the depth of their assimilation. For  example, there may be a consumer group that has a weak identification  to the dominant culture as well as their own culture; they may not be  proficient enough to understand English language advertising, but may   
 The Latino Influence on the U.S. Economy 35 

no longer rely on Spanish media for their information or entertainment.  This is a challenge for advertisers. Though challenging, some long held  beliefs still hold true; advertisers will not be all things to all people all  the time. So how can they break through to this multilayered Latino  population? 

Given the dearth of research outcomes regarding the effectiveness of  advertising methods on the multicultural Latino market, there has been  some analysis of what may be recommended, given the new attention to  acculturation and assimilation. Based on what has been presented in this  chapter, we can conclude that the degree of acculturation or assimilation  will affect the receptivity of advertising messages depending on the degree  of culturally sensitive images being presented in the advertisements. 

One could assume that a fully acculturated Latino group would  respond favorably to an Anglo targeted ad, as they identify more closely  with this adopted cultural representation. On the other end of the spec trum, a portion of the Latino population who have resisted adopting any  of the cultural aspects of the dominant society (speak Spanish exclusively  at home and in social and work situations), and adhere to the traditions  and culture of their heritage may only respond to Latino images and mes sages in an advertisement. This means Latino actors or representatives  with whom they share ethnic identification. Logic would again dictate  that for the very large Latino population who are acculturated, bicultural  advertising would probably be most effective. This hybrid approach not  only offers the benefit of communicating with this large and influential  consumer group but also serves to not offend any of the company’s Anglo  consumer groups. 

**The Latino Millennial** 

Millennials are a coveted buying group, because they have a very large  buying power and are the consumers of tomorrow. But they are not all the  same. Many companies and advertising firms have classified them or seg mented them based on behaviors, buying preferences, or any other char acteristic they find important. For instance, The Mercury Mambo Group  divides them into six categories: Hipennial, Gadget Guru, Millennial  Mom, Clean and Green Millennial, Anti-Millennial, and Old School.3  
36 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

Latino Millennials are interesting in that they still are closely aligned  with the mentality of immigrants, but they are also very comfortable in  the general population. They can easily traverse both worlds and mar keters can reach them through multiple channels and even in two lan guages. However, this group is still a different segment that cannot be  grouped into the general market. There are still some cultural differences  that make their needs, wants, and desires a bit more difficult to capture.  Viewed another way, they have unique characteristics that when identi fied make it easier to market to this group. 

From an innovation perspective, this group presents two opportuni ties. First, how do you reach them with products they judge to be innova tive? We will see later from our research that this group views innovation  as an improvement. It does not always have to be something new to grab  the attention of this demographic. The challenge for marketers is to then  structure their communication with this group accordingly. 

The second challenge with this group is to prepare them to go beyond  just attaining positions in the workforce. It is going beyond to put them  in positions where they can leverage their innovative capabilities: first,  preparing them early with the skills required in key positions; then pro 

viding mentorship for them to feel comfortable in the workplace and take  positions of leadership. 

**Summary** 

Latinos represent a significant market segment for many consumer oriented companies. The potential to grow this market is based on how  well companies can understand the shift in buying preferences and level  of acculturation.  
**CHAPTER 4** 

**Latino Potential for**    
**Innovation** 

The advent of technology has made it possible for businesses of all sizes  to compete on a global scale. The United States is now in competition  with companies from all over the world. Latin America has undergone  economic growth in recent years. The United States will stay competi 

tive by maintaining its innovative posture. Latinos are in a position to  be at the forefront of maintaining that competitive advantage. Thus, we  discuss competitive advantage and how to leverage an innovative Latino  workforce to compete with the world. 

**Sustained Competitive Advantage**  

**Through Innovation** 

For decades, the United States has been known as the world’s most inno vative country, because of its accomplishments in science and technology.  The rest of the world has emulated and benefitted from many of these  achievements, but there have also been many significant contributions  emerging from other regions. For decades, innovation was measured  exclusively through advances in R\&D and science for manufacturing  industries. 

However, as we begin to pay more attention to the benefits of apply ing innovation more broadly, we begin to see that innovation could be  applied effectively into service industries as well. Services are more people  oriented than tangible products; thus, it is critical to gain an understand ing of how individuals view and accept innovative solutions. As the rest  of the world has gained prominence through the outsourcing industry,  achieving competitive advantage is coming through the development of  an innovative workforce.  
38 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

In many countries, there is a concerted effort to develop the inno vative capabilities of their workforce by providing training and facili ties such as “innovation academies.” In Latin America, we have found  that most of the efforts for innovation still reside in the technology field.  It’s the technology companies that put in the most effort in delivering  innovation. Non-technical organizations offer innovative products and  services but more haphazardly. Many see innovation as critical but have  little experience in initiating an innovation project. This is different from  Asian countries and in particular Indian companies that are trying to  develop measurable innovation outcomes in Information Technology  (IT) Outsourcing as well as Business Process Outsourcing. Latinos and  innovation are two words that do not readily go together. This cannot  be said of groups, such as Asians, which are associated with innovation.  Is this a cultural phenomenon that crosses geographies or when Latinos  come to the United States, do they adjust to the innovation tendencies  they experience here? We believe it is the latter, but from an infrastructure  perspective there are still many areas that require attention to leverage this  capability in Latinos. Consequently, we do compare American Latinos  with professionals in Latin America to see if there are any commonalities. 

Advances in technology and the requirements to source materials and  talent from all over the world have created a business environment that  is global by definition. Competing in this environment requires com panies of all sizes to differentiate themselves and innovation is increas ingly identified as that differentiator. When corporations can establish  programs that lead to products and services that are judged to be innova tive, they have then established a competitive advantage in their industry.  But establishing this competitive advantage is challenging and sustaining  it is difficult. Modern enterprises have many resources they can manage  to achieve a competitive advantage through innovation, and none is more  important than their human capital. This means no innovation effort can  be successful without understanding and aligning how employees define  innovation. This is the true source of competitive advantage and does  merit some deeper discussion. 

Competitive advantage is simply the ability to do something better  than your competition. We see it among nations and we see it every day  in products and services. Competitive advantage in the context of this   
Latino Potential for Innovation 39 

book is based on leveraging the innovative capabilities of your workforce,  which will be increasingly composed of Latino workers. Globalization  and outsourcing have put additional pressure on nations to invest in  developing the skills of their workforce while upgrading their infrastruc 

ture. Along with this they have invested in leveraging and touting innova tion initiatives. Outsourcing has also expanded the need for innovation to  go beyond physical products, and instead gain an understanding of how  innovation is defined and implemented in the service industry. From the  marketing perspective, Latinos are viewed more as a source of revenue as  consumer brands continue to target this segment, and it is also viewed  as a source for voting constituency or low labor wages. That is, marketers  and businesses do not recognize the innovative capability of the Latino  consumer. 

Achieving competitive advantage through innovation is most eas ily possible through physical products, especially when they deliver in a  manner that, at best, astounds us. Latino innovations abound in the mar keting world. For instance, the most popular corn chips on the market  are those that have a Mexican theme. It was the influence of employees  working at the plants that produced the chips that provided this market ing innovation. 

For innovation to succeed, Latino businesses need core competencies  which are a combination of resources a company possesses that give it  a unique advantage in the marketplace, which ultimately provides sus tained competitive advantage. For any advantage to be sustainable and  not imitated by competitors, the resources and competencies that con tribute to this unique advantage must be idiosyncratic, that is, inimitable  and unique to that organization only. Latino businesses need to market  and exploit their uniqueness and their contributions to society in gen eral. They need to harness the power and potential of Latino employees  to innovate not only for their niche markets but also for the society in  general. Innovation must become a strategic component of a business  or organization, no matter what the ethnic characteristics. In order to  achieve superior performance, an organization must embrace “creative  destruction,” a departure from previous strategies, in which the mar ketplace becomes the impetus for the re-examination of processes. This  breeds the need for innovation, or new learning, and this ability becomes   
40 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

a new inimitable capability in and of itself. Not all organizations are  capable of departures from their entrenched business practices; therefore,  those organizations that possess a high capability to innovate will be more  responsive to environmental cues. That is what will propel them to supe 

rior performance through this unique competitive advantage. It is the  marketplace that ultimately makes established organizational paradigms  obsolete, but it is that dynamic process of developing internal resources  that continually yields positions of market superiority despite the actions  of competitors that only innovation can provide. 

Innovation has been presented as the core competency an organi zation must possess to achieve sustainable competitive advantage, and  consequently, superior financial performance. However, when the mar ketplace shifts in its wants and needs, most if not all of the competitors in  that marketplace want to be the first to address this new reality. Some will  succeed, some will not. Latino businesses can adopt an innovative stra tegic focus for the company to effectively and accurately interpret what  is needed at this juncture. The business can either choose to react or not  react with an offering that achieves lasting competitive advantage. These  organizations are responding to customer wants and needs. This is a strat egy that will work for Latino businesses. 

Competitive advantage has its roots in both the competitor and cus tomer dimensions. Sustainable competitive advantage is derived from  those skills and resources inherent within the firm that resist erosion by  competitors, and these resources manifest in the form of long-term supe rior business performance. Therefore, the Latino business should engage  in problem solving activities, such as recognition of the disparity between  what is and what should or could be, and a review of which resources the  organization can dedicate to this opportunity in response. This activity of  problem identification and ultimately problem resolution is where inno vation can manifest itself. However, there has to be an intervening factor  that filters this information from the market (whether it be the customers  directly or the competition’s response to the customers) through to the  innovative response mechanism, and then into a manageable process. 

Market orientation is doing something new or different in response to  market conditions or having an external focus and interpretation mecha nism. Therefore, innovation is poised as that necessary component in the   
Latino Potential for Innovation 41 

process to be that something new, something changed, or something dif ferent, as per the findings of Global Targeting’s Project Impact research.  Market orientation, basically serving as information processing, is the  impetus for innovation success. Markets are rarely stagnant, because there  is always new data emerging on trends, ideas, competitors, and other  external influencers that present challenges and opportunities for compa nies. Latino businesses and organizations can integrate the development  of an organization’s strategy for performance enhancement. Performance  enhancement is a critical lynchpin for recognizing innovation from an  individual perspective. Enhancements are capable of a seemingly constant  state of paradigm disruption to accommodate new ideas and opportuni ties as the market dictates. These organizations may experience success  initially in response to a selected opportunity, but may not be able to  reposition itself again in the short, or even long term. 

Unstable or unanticipated environmental circumstances are oppor tunities for organizations to call upon their internal capabilities (i.e.,  “core competencies”) and capitalize on market triggers and produce  innovations, whether they are in the form of something new, something  changed, or something different. It is an organization’s capability to do  this on an ongoing basis that contributes to enhancing business perfor mance, and ultimately, sustained competitive advantage. In the truest  sense of the word, imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, and in the  marketplace, competitors embrace this idea; nothing attracts more atten tion than success, and competitors will often resort to imitation rather  than innovation to maintain their position in the market, and their per formance objectives. 

The discussion on competitive advantage took us through a generic  scenario. Now we need to make it specific and show how it applies to  Latinos. As a group, Latinos will play a significant part in how the world  economy will develop from a U.S. perspective. This is not because of  any amount of collective wealth accumulation, but because of the impact  they are having on the Americas. A major factor for the growth of the  United States is the influx of immigrants. Throughout the decades,  many have come to the United States in mass numbers, speaking a dif ferent language, and eventually being absorbed into the Anglo culture  that dominates the United States. Others have come to the United States   
42 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

and have left elements of their culture embedded into society. But once  those immigrants have established themselves and throughout the years  become fully acculturated in the United States, ties to their homeland  are dissipated with each subsequent generation. Although it is yet to be  determined in which direction Latinos will go, this does not seem to be  the case with Latinos. 

The destiny of Latinos is at a crossroad between immigration and  globalization. On the one hand, businesses with a global footprint have  expanded along with the ability of many countries to become viable hosts  or destinations of choice, which has impacted the United States’ posi 

tion of pre-eminence. On the other hand, can the United States continue  to attract immigrants in the same numbers they have in the past from  LatAm? Most of these countries are investing in their infrastructure and  are now keeping more of its citizens at home. How competitive the United  States remains will depend on the people they keep, train, and develop  to achieve their best innovative capabilities. nication. The geographical proximity and trade with Latin America also  continues to exert influence on American society. nies hire bilingual customer service representatives. It would appear that

this represents an opportunity for bilingual professionals to build their  career and credentials—and it certainly is. But also consider that many  of these same firms have the option to relocate and build these centers in  LatAm. Whereas this once represented an opportunity for bilingual U.S.- 

based professionals to manage these centers, this is instead competition in  terms of destination selection and talent. 

Technology has changed the business landscape. The ability to reach  customers on multiple continents is no longer the exclusive domain of  large firms. Sourcing products, customers, natural resources, and stag ing areas or access points is more complex, fluid, and requires a shift in  organizational business models. To understand the next steps for implementing innovation, leadership  needs to focus on improving innovation skills among employees.
