tives need to harness the talent present to make this a reality. This chapter  has demonstrated the need for innovation and why it offers a distinctive  competitive advantage.  
**CHAPTER 5** 

**Research Results and**    
**Practical Implications** 

In this chapter, we provide you with our primary research on Latino  attitudes, opinions, and disposition toward innovation. We take you  through the statistical analyses that helped shape our views on innova tion. This is research from the Project Impact study, and it looks at data  from U.S. Latinos and a consolidated view from various countries in  Latin America. We present the two separately and offer a comparative  view of both as well. 

**Introduction** 

There are many challenges associated with innovation. How to do it?  What processes to choose? What type of innovation is best? These are  all good questions and necessary to answer at one point or another. But  before taking on any kind of innovation endeavor, it is of the utmost  importance to define innovation and get to the meaning of the term.  In our daily conversations and exposure to advertising, we are presented  with multiple interpretations and meaning of the term. It appears there  is not a standard approach that can be taken without actually finding out  how it is viewed, interpreted, and valued. 

The problem lies in that the word “innovation” means many different  things to many different people. If you research the word in the diction ary, you will find that the most common definition uses two keywords:  “new” and “novel.” An innovation is a new idea or novel (unique) concept.  Innovation, from our perspective, uses this definition and expands on its  meaning. To begin, inventions are certainly innovations. They change our  lives; they transform the way we do things; they shift the boundaries of  our knowledge. The U.S. Patent Office receives numerous applications   
46 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

each day to protect inventions; but to most people these innovations are  unique and special—not something thought of as ordinary. Inventions  occur irregularly and are heralded as groundbreaking, when a need exists  for the invention. They are truly special events—not often repeated or  replicated. For many, the “holy grail” for continuous innovation is a strat 

egy that imitates and sustains innovation on a regular basis. That strategy  would not restrict innovations to only “new” items but also include inno vations that improve products, services, and technology. In fact, the term  could easily apply to people and decisions that have resulted in a positive  outcome. That is, innovation has a much broader definition than is often  applied to it.1 

A scholarly researcher found over 60 individual definitions of the  word innovation.2 We know the word innovation has many meanings.  Some see innovation as a novel idea. Yet, in reality, innovation is more  than new ideas; it is new technology, new ways of operating, and new  ways of managing. Innovation occurs when humans employ a creative  process to meet a particular need; innovation begins at a very human  level. You could even call this the “Atomic” level.3 Therefore, a correct  definition should include the contribution of human beings to address a  need with available resources. Innovation begins at the human level with a  creative thought and a reason to fulfill an important need, want, or desire. 

From our study and empirical research, we arrived at a definition  that describes innovation from a perspective of what the innovation  will accomplish. This will help to better clarify how individuals perceive  (understand) innovation. People are familiar with outcomes (these are  tangible products, services, or processes). We have a whole set of out 

comes that we use to judge whether a product, process, or service is truly  innovative. Our experiences tell us when something is better or improved,  especially when that “item” undergoes change to meet our needs. We  judge this “item” as innovative when it better meets our needs. In the  Latino market, we see innovations all the time, but often these innova 

tions are not fully recognized or accepted. Businesses market these prod ucts, services, and technology without the innovation label. This outcome  results in lost competitive advantage. Individuals will recognize innova tion from their experience and use, given that the item meets a need,  want, or desire.  
Research Results and Practical Implications 47 

In order to clarify a definition of innovation that will relate to an  individual’s understanding, Baregheh, Rowley, and Sambrook4 decided to  examine the “means of innovation” (p. 1334); that is, understanding how  innovation “transforms ideas into new, improved, or changed” (p. 1334\)  items, services, or people. From this definition and our research, we  arrived at three unique descriptors of innovation that transforms objects  (things) to meet new or different needs. 

We use three descriptive words to define how innovation trans forms objects (things/items). The three main descriptors or themes are  new, improved, or change that describes how the product, technology,  or service is transformed. In other words, how the product, service, or  technology is “transformed” into something we define as innovative, as it  better meets our needs, wants, and desires. There is a distinctive strategy  for each of the three descriptors. This makes sense, since most leaders  and managers are interested in innovation from a perspective of what it  will accomplish. When a customer or user experiences a product, service  or technology designed to exceed more than what they expect, they will  identify this as true innovation. As expectations change, so do our needs. 

Congratulate yourself if you felt that the meaning of innovation was  something more than an invention\! You are the best judge of whether  something is innovative or not. Where we differ from most is that innova tion is more than something new; it is more than a creative idea or new  technology; it is a means to meet a need (new or existing) with something  better than what presently exists. 

Think about the Apple iPad (version 4 as of this writing)—is this  innovative? Well, if we used the standard terms of innovation—is it new  technology or new to the marketplace? Is it a repackage of the tablet PC  or a new update? Whatever you believe it to be, it is innovative as it spe 

cifically addresses a need. We define innovation from its ability to meet  a human need. The fact is that the iPad is innovative without being very  new (obviously it has some new hardware/software or technology) or  novel. 

Consider a second piece of technology, the Microsoft Surface. Is the  Surface truly new or novel or an improvement on existing technology?  Given that the “tablet” became popular beginning in the early 2000s, is  it truly something new or unique or rather quite an improvement over its   
48 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

predecessor? We believe that most people will in fact say that their tablet  today is an improvement over what existed previously. That being the  case, the iPad or Surface tablet is innovative as it fulfills many needs as  compared to its existing competition. Innovation occurs numerous times  when improvements or changes occur to an existing technology, product,  or service. 

**Defining the “Means” of Innovation** 

As mentioned previously, innovation consists of three distinct themes,  concepts, or categories. Each concept or theme describes the innovation  transformation. The innovation (its definition individualized) transforms  into three distinctive themes or dimensions. Think of these as three dis 

tinctive methods or ways of accomplishing the same goal, innovation.  For example, consider that stocks, bonds, or commodities are methods or  ways to invest money. All accomplish the same goal (hopefully), classified  by the type of investment. Each investment type requires a unique (and  often related) strategy. Innovation follows the same pattern: 

1\. Theme 1: ***New*** (something new or a novel \[unique\] idea)—normally  we think of new technology. 

2\. Theme 2: ***Improvement*** (making something better)—this relates to  products, processes or services. Improvement is for those products,  processes, or services that are underperforming. 

3\. Theme 3: ***Change*** (replacing what presently exists for something dif ferent)—affects people both physically and emotionally. Innovative  change is positive change benefitting the organization.5 

Each theme is distinctive, yet inter-related, as all need the individual  to initiate the innovation. What is different is how individuals perceive  their importance. Of all the three themes, innovative change is not widely  acknowledged. This is probably the most overlooked aspect of innova 

tion. We believe this is where Global Targeting has its greatest opportu nity. Making change positive is truly innovative as it directly affects us  all. Surprisingly, people frequently recognize it as being the most impor tant and significant theme (descriptor) of innovation. Think back when   
Research Results and Practical Implications 49 

change occurred in your job, your boss, or your life—was it positive— did it make a difference? Did it change you for the better? If it did, it  was innovative. Of course, a negative experience may have also changed  you. If the eventual outcome was positive, then the change is innovative.  Of course, a negative experience could easily lead to a negative outcome  that defines destructive change. Negative experiences can also result from  destructive change—change made with a negative intent. Many times  the situation warrants a negative outcome, but the process, the commu 

nications, and the repercussions can lead to destructive change. Destruc tive changes affect morale, motivation, and productivity issues. These are  in fact, anti-innovative and the consequences and repercussions may be  devastating. 

Each theme or transformation continuously defines what the innova tion will accomplish. When we “define” innovation, we use these terms,  not as a definition but more about expectations (related to experiences)  and perceptions (how we judge something). Remember, innovation  begins and ends with the individual. When we look at this as a collec tive body of people, we can see certain cultural traits and trends that will  require alignment. If we experience something better than expected and  if it meets more of our needs, then we say it is innovative. Innovativeness  increases as more needs are met. 

Through our Project Impact study, we have scientifically validated  these three themes (means) of innovation with numerous cultural and  ethnic groups worldwide. What is interesting is that each cultural group  identifies the three themes; however, the strongest theme varies from  group to group (culture to culture). Using the research data, described  in this chapter, specifically geared to Latinos, we identified three dis 

tinct demographic categories (gender, generation, and job function) and  found that no significant differences exist between genders but do exist  between generations and job functions. Technical individuals tend to  understand innovation very differently than non-technical individuals.  Technical individuals place a higher priority on the new dimension of  innovation; non-technical individuals place more priority on change and  improvements. Even more significant was the difference between three  generations (Millennials born between 1980 and 1998; Generation X  born between 1964 and 1979; and the Baby Boomer Generation born   
50 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

between 1946 and 1964). These generations take a very different view of  innovation by applying a unique priority ranking for the three themes.  The result could lead to a potential conflict in team dynamics when work ing on innovation projects, given how individuals understand innova tion. There is nothing more compelling than asking individuals to define  innovation and listening to the various definitions that both complement  and conflict with one another. Various conflicting definitions, expressed  by their employees, have shocked many of those in authority. Given the  diversity of opinion, it is easy to understand how conflict, dissent, and  disengagement cripple the chances for success. 

**Perceiving Innovation** 

We all perceive innovation with knowledge, experience and an under standing of whether a product, service, or technology performs (see  Figure 5.1). If our needs are met beyond what we have experienced previ ously, we designate the “item” as innovative. Once we build up enough  information on an object, we can judge any changes that occur and from  that determine whether those changes are innovative. From a business  perspective, we cannot know how each person perceives something as  innovative. What we can do is to determine how much a product, service,  or technology requires a transformation in order for a majority of people  to recognize it as innovative. We previously mentioned the Business Inno vation Ecosystem (BIE) as a way for companies to have sustained innova tion success. Reaching out to customers is a key element. Ultimately they  decide what is innovative. 

Transformations can take many forms. It could be a new and unique  technology, a vastly improved product, or a significant change to person nel. Companies and organizations that transform their offerings without  first considering their customer (user) needs, wants, and desires will often  fail. It is not enough to “make something better”; it requires the product,  technology, process, or service to meet more than existing needs. That is,  it must add value. Customers respond (by purchasing) when their needs  are better met. Meeting new needs or refining needs met previously can  accomplish the same objective. The “trick” is finding the balance between  meeting needs, wants, and desires and determining the amount of   
Research Results and Practical Implications 51 

transformation an object requires. Knowing what to transform provides  the business or organization a real competitive advantage. For new products, services, or technologies, often business lead ers begin with a small group of innovators who will familiarize people  with a new or improved product. A perfect example of this is the Apple  iPad that essentially replaced the tablet PC. What made the iPad innova tive was that it met more needs than its predecessor. This is why we say  that when you increase the needs met, you are also going to increase the  number of purchases. For the Apple iPad, it was a small group—the so called pioneers, or Early Adopters in marketing terms, that invested in the  iPad. When the product filled more needs or desires (such as size, weight,  function, and so forth), they proclaimed the iPad as a new innovation.  The pioneers “transformed” perceptions of what a product such as the  iPad can accomplish and specifically how it met more needs. Many times  communications, marketing, and advertising favorably transform per ceptions. However, unless the business meets more needs, it will not be  perceived as innovative. Transforming perceptions is not enough—as the  physical product, process, technology, or service must perform beyond  present expectations. 

Although the iPad does contain new technology for the most part,  it is purely a replacement for the more traditional tablet PC. Of course,  there will be some individuals whose needs are met but see that the per formance of the product, service, or technology has improved and thus  identifies this as innovation. Innovation is not just about meeting or  exceeding needs, but it is also about meeting or exceeding performance.  At times, we find that people identify innovation is purely performance driven as the object meets all critical needs. We also know that individuals  identify improvement when the need is met in a realistic timeframe. It  is best to understand that people will perceive something as innovative  because it exceeds the performance of something with which they have  experience. Again, for businesspeople, it is not important to try to make  everyone recognize that what they offer, what they sell, is innovative.  What is more important is to understand that the organization should be  addressing what a customer or user needs, and how the product, service,  or technology that they produce can either meet needs or deliver better  performance.

**Results of Latino Study** 

Much of the data we have provided to support our position thus far has  been based on secondary sources, that is, the validated work of others. But  when it comes to innovation and the impact culture has on it, we are pro viding primary data. This is where we provide our own work to expand  upon what others are doing, or to build support for our management  

models. In this chapter, we will share our findings with you. When you mention the word “research,” people often think of sci entific or medical research—research conducted in the laboratory using  sophisticated instruments and computer software. Research actually has  a much broader meaning than just traditional scientific-related activities.  Research exists outside of science, medicine, or technology. For busi nesses, it is critical to understand the purchasing behaviors of individuals  to segment markets appropriately; therefore, we study their perceptions  and beliefs. Organizations gather this information to help predict behav iors. Whatever the form of research, it is important to note that there is    
Research Results and Practical Implications 53 

a strict adherence to numerous guidelines to ensure that the results are  trustworthy and that the research meets ethical guidelines. One common form of research familiar to many businesspeople is that  of marketing research. Market research has the goal of collecting infor mation to help marketing professionals understand and improve purchas ing behavior—the key phrase being “to understand.” Research provides a  unique method to capture, clarify, and summarize this information. The  information we seek is how individuals understand and react to innova tion. Given that innovation improves competitive advantage, we devel oped a research plan to study how Latinos understand innovation and how  it affects their purchasing behavior and ability to develop products and ser vices to meet market demands. This also applies to leading Latino talent. Of course, we could have chosen to collect this data in a non-scientific  manner and the results presented would have had questionable use. Often,  many take this approach to save time or expense of conducting research.  Unfortunately, when appropriate scientific and ethical research practices  are not considered, there is room for bias and incorrect interpretation.  We see this all the time in polling data during election time. Often, both  parties take polls that are not scientific and then try to interpret them  as if they had scientific validity. Data collected without specific controls  may contain errors or be biased. That is, the data is of little value before it  is analyzed. This is why we state up front that the research conducted in  a scientific manner greatly increases believability. We want to assure our  readers that the results presented here provide valid information about the  respondents who participated in this research. We do not claim that this  will explain or describe all Latino adults. What it does accomplish is that  it provides factual data on how these individuals (respondents) under stand innovation and what it means to them personally, thus allowing us  to provide a balanced perspective. 

**The Need to Interpret the Numbers** 

People react very differently to numbers. Either, they trust the numbers or  distrust the numbers implicitly. We understand why people distrust num bers and specifically statistics, given the fact that the numbers are often  invalid or unpredictable. There is a risk, sometimes quite large, that data   
54 LEADING LATINO TALENT TO CHAMPION INNOVATION 

collected in an unprofessional manner robs the data of its validity and  reliability. What this means to you is that data often contains errors which  are then interpreted incorrectly resulting in poor or incorrect analysis. We  definitely want you to feel comfortable with the numbers and the analysis  we present. As we stated in the first section, applying scientific research  principles increases the believability of our results. We promise not to  overextend the results to include forecasts or statements that the data can not support. What we will promise is that the numbers and specifically  the data analysis are valid for the sample collected. It is impossible to sam 

ple everyone and in fact, this is why we use techniques such as random  sampling. There is always some error and risk in how one interprets data,  but we also understand that we can minimize that risk through effective  data collection procedures and error checking. Inevitably, the \$64,000  question is what the data reveals about the Latino population sampled. 

It is our intent to assure you that the results are believable and trustwor thy. What the data reveals is that there are distinctive patterns and trends  with this particular ethnic group. That is not to say that everyone in this  group believes or subscribes to the same understanding of innovation. What  it does say is that the results demonstrate a great deal of consistency. What  this means for you, our reader, is that you can apply these results to Latino  knowledge workers presently in the workforce, and perhaps help in develop ing the next generation entering the workforce. Although employees work ing in innovative intensive industries dominate the data, the similarities to  those non-technical employees confirm that applicability to a wider audi ence. That is, basic patterns persist for technical and non-technical employ ees across the entire sample. The assumption we make is that technical  individuals employed in industries other than IT-related will share a com mon understanding of innovation. Our Project Impact studies conducted  on a global basis confirm much the same information as this data set. There fore, we state that our results apply to Latinos outside of the sampled group. 

Interpreting the data requires an understanding of this ethnic group  and its distinctive characteristics. We base our interpretation on knowl edge and experience with this group combined with experience in  interpreting statistical output. We present no statistical analysis, only a  synthesis of the results and an evaluation of its meaning in common sense language. This type of data collection does not “prove” anything   
Research Results and Practical Implications 55 

but explains and confirms certain patterns and behaviors. This leaves you,  our reader, with the ability to agree with our data analysis or to examine  the data and interpret it differently depending upon your experience and  familiarity with this group.
